lessons.title: Where contamination comes from
lessons.html:
Meat is a perfect home for bacteria

The muscle of a healthy animal is almost free of bacteria. Contamination happens during slaughter and dressing. Bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli and Listeria can make people seriously ill. As a supervisor you must know where contamination comes from so you can stop it.

Main sources

  • Hide, hair, wool and skin: dirty animals carry dung and soil. Contamination happens when the hide is opened and pulled off.
  • Gut content: spilled rumen or intestine content during evisceration is very high risk.
  • Workers: dirty hands, clothes and knives, and sick workers.
  • Equipment: knives, saws, hooks, tables and trays not cleaned and sterilised.
  • Environment: condensation, dirty walls, splashing from floors, pests.
  • Water: water used in the abattoir must be potable (fit to drink).

Cross-contamination

Cross-contamination means bacteria move from a dirty item to a clean one. Examples: a worker touches the hide and then the meat; a knife cuts through dung and then into meat; a carcass rubs against a dirty one; clean and dirty workers walk through the same doors.

Clean and dirty areas

Abattoirs separate dirty areas (lairage, stunning, bleeding, hide removal, gut room) from clean areas (dressed carcass line, chillers, deboning, dispatch). Workers, equipment and air should move from clean to dirty, never back. Different colours of overalls or helmets often show which area a worker belongs to.

lessons.title: Hygienic slaughter and dressing practices
lessons.html:
Good practice on the line

Animals

  • Only clean, dry animals should go to slaughter. Very dirty animals may need to be washed in the lairage and allowed to drip dry, or slaughtered last.
  • Rest and water in the lairage reduce stress.

Dressing

  • Use the two-knife system where required: one knife cuts while the other is in the steriliser.
  • Open the hide from the inside out so hair does not touch the meat.
  • Tie or clip the oesophagus (rodding) and bag and tie the bung (rectum) before evisceration so gut content cannot leak.
  • Do not cut into stomachs or intestines during evisceration.
  • Keep carcasses apart on the rail.
  • Trim visible contamination with a clean knife. Do not just wash it, because washing spreads bacteria.

Personal hygiene

  • Clean protective clothing every shift; hair nets or helmets.
  • No jewellery, watches or false nails.
  • Wash hands on entering, after the toilet, after touching hides or dirty items, and whenever needed.
  • No eating, smoking or chewing gum in production areas.
  • Cuts covered with waterproof coloured plasters and gloves.
  • Workers with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or infected wounds report sick and do not handle meat.

Equipment

Knife sterilisers must be kept at the temperature set in your procedures and checked with a thermometer. Hand wash basins must have hot water, soap and paper towels. Report broken equipment immediately.

lessons.title: Hygiene management systems and supervision
lessons.html:
A system, not just rules

Under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 an abattoir must manage hygiene through a documented system. This usually includes a hygiene management plan, standard operating procedures, cleaning schedules, pest control, water testing, temperature records and training records. Many abattoirs use HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) principles.

HACCP in simple terms

  1. Identify the hazards (biological, chemical, physical) at each step.
  2. Find the critical control points where a hazard can be controlled, for example chilling.
  3. Set limits, such as the maximum carcass temperature before dispatch.
  4. Monitor each control point.
  5. Take corrective action when a limit is not met.
  6. Verify that the system works, for example by microbiological testing.
  7. Keep records.

Microbiological testing

Swabs of carcass surfaces and equipment are sent to a laboratory. The results show whether hygiene is working. A rising bacterial count on carcasses tells you something is going wrong, even if the meat looks clean.

The supervisor's daily role

  • Check that workers follow hygiene rules and correct them on the spot.
  • Check records are complete and signed.
  • Lead by example: wash your hands and wear protective clothing correctly.
  • Explain why rules matter; workers follow rules they understand.

Key points

  • Hides, gut content, workers, equipment and the environment are the main sources of contamination.
  • Keep clean and dirty areas separate and move from clean to dirty.
  • Trim visible contamination rather than washing it off.
  • Sick workers must not handle meat.
  • HACCP principles identify and control hazards at critical points.

Why is the bung (rectum) bagged and tied before evisceration?
